For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

text.text: Patient-clinician interactions are central to diagnosis and treatment in mental health care.
They involve inferential processes grounded in patients' reports of symptoms and clinicians' interpretations of signs.
These processes are liable to microdynamic looping effects that drive diagnostic belief formation.

In facing the epistemic challenge of reaching a shared ascription of the patient's condition, such looping effects can lead to misalignment and give rise to epistemic injustice if a credibility deficit exists between the patient and the clinician.

In this paper, we use the active inference framework to develop a computational model of looping microdynamics that captures how patients and clinicians reciprocally interpret symptoms, attribute causes, and negotiate diagnostic categories over time.

We present a simulation study showing how specific interactional patterns can amplify or mitigate credibility deficits, depending in part on clinicians' attributional attitudes toward patients' self-interpretations.

Our results suggest that, in contexts of diagnostic disagreement, positive disconfirmationoffering an alternative explanatory framing rather than simply negating the patient's perspective-may reduce the risk of epistemic injustice.

Overall, the model highlights how looping microdynamics structure mutual belief formation in clinical encounters and how attention to these dynamics can support more epistemically responsible clinical communication.
Looping effects can occur at many levels in mental health, psychiatry and psychology.

They can occur in the construction of categories and concepts that become ways that people identify and understand themselves; in institutional practices that deploy diagnostic systems that shape illness experience; and in the dynamics of the clinical encounter (Brinkmann, 2005; Gillespie & Wagoner, 2025; Kirmayer, 2026; Kirmayer & Sartorius, 2007).

>LOOPING EFFECTS AND EPISTEMIC INJUSTICES
text.formatted: <head n="2." >LOOPING EFFECTS AND EPISTEMIC INJUSTICES</head>

text.text: Mental health assessments involve communicative interactions between patients and clinicians.
Like any interpersonal interaction, this process can change the cognition and experience of both interlocutors.
In clinical settings, this interaction shapes the ways in which patients recollect and present their symptoms and distress -and the ways that clinicians respond.
This interactional process may introduce biases that change patients' symptom presentations over time, sometimes in unpredictable ways.

This can happen when clinicians emphasize certain aspects of the patient's experience through questions (e.g., "Can you tell me more about your fatigue?") and responses, which may be shaped by clinicians' theoretical orientation, models of psychopathology, or other aspects of their background (Kirmayer, 2025).
text.formatted: This can happen when clinicians emphasize certain aspects of the patient's experience through questions (e.g., "Can you tell me more about your fatigue?") and responses, which may be shaped by clinicians' theoretical orientation, models of psychopathology, or other aspects of their background <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">(Kirmayer, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: The clinician's questions may direct the patient's attention to specific symptoms or illness schemas related to causal attributions or implicit models (e.g., "Yes, now that I think about it, my fatigue is related to my backache and it's especially bad on weekdays, when I am really stressed at work").

This in turn may provide the patient with motivations to use local cultural idioms of distress to make sense of their experience, thus emphasizing a given configuration of the presentation often accompanied of an explanation or schema (e.g., "I think I'm suffering from burnout") (Kirmayer & Young, 1998; Macias-Velasquez et al., 2020).
text.formatted: This in turn may provide the patient with motivations to use local cultural idioms of distress to make sense of their experience, thus emphasizing a given configuration of the presentation often accompanied of an explanation or schema (e.g., "I think I'm suffering from burnout") <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">(Kirmayer & Young, 1998;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">Macias-Velasquez et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: In his earlier work, Ian Hacking (1985) framed these self-constituting and vindicating effects of diagnostic practices in terms of a larger process that he termed the "looping effect of human kinds" (i.e., the fact that people change their self-ascription and experience in response to the categories and descriptions they live under, and the fact that these categories change, in turn, as a function of people's subsequent (shared) experience).

text.text: Though Hacking provided detailed historical studies of the looping effect in psychiatric phenomena (Hackinghttps://paperpile.com/c/1lHXLs/VF1H3+RBbca 1998a (Hacking, , 1998b)) , he was not primarily concerned with the mechanisms of looping.

text.text: In a useful essay, he noted that looping processes involve large-scale discursive formations of power/knowledge; like those described by Foucault as well as the microdynamics of situated interpersonal interaction studied by sociologists like Erving Goffman (Hacking, 2004).
text.formatted: In a useful essay, he noted that looping processes involve large-scale discursive formations of power/knowledge; like those described by Foucault as well as the microdynamics of situated interpersonal interaction studied by sociologists like Erving Goffman <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Hacking, 2004)</ref>.

text.text: These macro and micro dynamics interact by creating and (de)stabilizing categories in social and cultural institutions and practices.

Building on this dual (macro/micro) view of looping effects, Gauld and colleagues (2025) proposed a mechanistic account -in the context of clinical interactions -that distinguishes two temporal scales of looping effects, according to which changes in patients' presentations at short time scales would be explained by "microdynamic" looping effects based on the capacity of patients to experience change in symptoms through processes of self-construal.

text.text: Ensuing institutional nosological revision would be explained by "macrodynamic" looping effects on a longer time scale, based on the capacity of the medical institution to revise its nosology in response to clinicians' cumulative experience of new presentations emerging from communicative interactions.

In their paper, Gauld and colleagues address the epistemic nature of these looping processes and the need to better understand the dynamics of looping in a clinical setting, since they may lead to epistemic injustices that disrupt the clinical relation and harm the patient.
Fricker (2007) identified two types of epistemic injustice, testimonial and hermeneutical.

We adopt Amandine Catala's (Catala, 2025; Catala et al., 2021) terminological clarification and analysis of the theory of epistemic injustice according to which an epistemic injustice occurs when a person suffers the consequences of an undue credibility deficit (testimonial injustice) or of an undue intelligibility deficit (hermeneutical injustice).
text.formatted: We adopt Amandine Catala's <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Catala, 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">Catala et al., 2021)</ref> terminological clarification and analysis of the theory of epistemic injustice according to which an epistemic injustice occurs when a person suffers the consequences of an undue credibility deficit (testimonial injustice) or of an undue intelligibility deficit (hermeneutical injustice).

text.text: Testimonial injustices happen, for instance, when an interlocutor (here, the clinician) disregards the testimony of a contributor (e.g., failing to consult a patient who could competently contribute to the exchange).
In certain circumstances, the situation is such that the contributor cannot even attempt to contribute.
These are cases of "silencing", or "pre-emptive" testimonial injustice.

In turn, hermeneutical injustices happen when contributors either remain misunderstood by an interlocutor (i.e., self-to-others intelligibility) or fails to understand their own situation (i.e., self-to-self intelligibility) due to an intelligibility deficit.

According to Catala (2025), sources of intelligibility deficits include the lack of concepts in the common pool of meaning making resources capturing the contributor's experience, the rejection by the interlocutors of the meaning making resources of the contributor, or the misunderstanding by the locutor of existing meaning making resources.
text.formatted: According to <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">Catala (2025)</ref>, sources of intelligibility deficits include the lack of concepts in the common pool of meaning making resources capturing the contributor's experience, the rejection by the interlocutors of the meaning making resources of the contributor, or the misunderstanding by the locutor of existing meaning making resources.

text.text: Below, we present simulations of patient-clinician interactions under conditions that feature a "credibility deficit."

The patient can contribute to the interaction, but their contribution has no effect on the clinician's understanding of the patient's situation, thereby reflecting a case of testimonial injustices, where the patient is not, overtly silenced or precluded from contributing, but where the effect of contribution is nullified, given the interactional setting.
For the sort of Bayesian agents implemented here, this credibility deficit can lead to interactions posing risks of intelligibility deficits and associated hermeneutical injustices.

For instance, the clinician may hear the patient say "I am feeling sad", and respond "No, what you experience is anxiety", thereby leading to a loss of confidence in the patient model, the model reflecting a belief of the sort "Ah, OK, but then I'm not sure of what I feel anymore".

Accordingly, in this simulation, the intelligibility deficit arises from the inability of the patient to contribute to the meaning-making process implicit in the patient-clinician interaction (e.g., the clinician failing to take seriously the patient's resistance to their assessment).

Practically, the patient model will suffer a credibility deficit in the sense that their testimonial contribution to the interaction will be attenuated under the conditions instantiating the credibility deficit.

The consequence of this is that the shared reality between the clinician and the patient will become increasingly divorced from the patient's interpretation of their own situation, thereby leading to an intelligibility deficit.
Note, also, that credibility imbalances often are created by credibility gaps in which the credibility of the contributor is reduced, while that of the interlocutor is increased (Medina, 2011).

text.text: In our simulation, there will be no increased credibility of the interlocutor under the credibility deficit conditions.
Only a decrease of credibility on the side of the contributor.

Our simulation aims to understand the mechanisms of looping microdynamics that underwrite joint inference based upon shared and communicated observations, as well as the consequence these microdynamics have on epistemic injustices in clinical context.
To simulate the kind of belief updating implicated in looping microdynamics we will use the Bayesian mechanics afforded by active inference.

In particular, we address the interpretative problem faced by doctors and patients resolved under a shared generative models or narratives and, crucially, a reciprocal influence of both participants in a dyadic interaction (Friston & Frith, 2015; Frith & Wentzer, 2013).
text.formatted: In particular, we address the interpretative problem faced by doctors and patients resolved under a shared generative models or narratives and, crucially, a reciprocal influence of both participants in a dyadic interaction <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Friston & Frith, 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">Frith & Wentzer, 2013)</ref>.

text.text: This requisite reciprocity will be studied in terms of a credibility deficit in which the doctor fails to assign credibility or precision to the patient's contribution exposing the patient to a risk of hermeneutical injustice.
The scenario we implement is an interaction between two mutually influencing cognitive agents engaged in communicative exchange.
One agent represents the clinician, and the other represents the patient.

The task of the two agents is to infer the category that fits the patient's situation (e.g., diagnostic category A or B), and to predict the symptom associated with the category (e.g., reports of sadness or anxiety).
For the patient, this corresponds to the "subjective" framing of their situation (e.g., "I have A") and to reflecting upon their experience (e.g., "I am sad").

For the clinician, the inference corresponds to the "subjective" formulation of a preliminary diagnosis (e.g., "The patient might have B"), and to the "subjective" perception of symptoms (e.g., "I see sadness").
In our model, the diagnostic category must be inferred because it is a latent variable.

Conversely, the symptom is something that is observed and shared through the patient's selfreport, which forms the basis of diagnostic inference -and implicitly, a shared commitment between the patient and doctor to a common understanding of the symptoms at hand.
We will also commit to the conventional clinical distinction between a "symptom" and a "sign".
A symptom is something the patient reports, whereas a sign is something that a clinician observes.
The symptom is expected to track the underlying experience of the patient, while functioning as an indicator of the patient's diagnostic category.
However, in practice, there may be a mismatch between the reported symptom and the patient's experience (e.g., as in the case of autistic masking or due to the clinician's pre-theoretic assumptions).

The model on offer in this paper makes the simplifying assumption that, from the point of view of the clinician, there is a lawful (i.e., deterministic) mapping between the experience and the symptom.
By contrast, the mapping between symptoms and diagnostic categories is probabilistic as the model allows for uncertainty in the likelihood of each symptom given the diagnostic category.

The mutual influence between the patient and the clinician occurs through the communicative interaction, or exchange of "observable" information mediated by an "objective" process that can be influenced by the actions of the patient and the clinician (Bruineberg et al., 2018).

text.text: The objective process corresponds to the process generating observations in the context of an interaction between the patient and doctor.
Thus, we will call this the "interaction" process.

The interaction process includes the objective symptom-category likelihood mappings, about which both the patient and clinician have prior beliefs (called their subjective modelhttps://paperpile.com/c/1lHXLs/Y7f3b (Schwartenbeck & Friston, 2016 ).
text.formatted: The interaction process includes the objective symptom-category likelihood mappings, about which both the patient and clinician have prior beliefs (called their subjective model) <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">(Schwartenbeck & Friston, 2016</ref> <ref type="url" target="https://paperpile.com/c/1lHXLs/Y7f3b">)</ref>.

text.text: An interactional process can be understood in terms of a shared generative structure that encodes probabilistic dependencies between inferred states and future observations, thus mediating the temporal coupling between (joint) belief updating, and subsequent symptom expression.
Our model assumes that all patient-clinician interactions take place within this shared interaction process.

In the case of the patient, the communicated information that shapes the interaction is about their symptom experience and their beliefs about the associated category (e.g., "I think I have A because I am sad").
For the clinician, the interaction process shaping communicative interaction involves confirming or contradicting the patient's claim (e.g., "A does not cause sadness").
As a preliminary step, to characterize the convergence properties of the model, we simulated 1000 interactions (trials) per condition, for 9 different conditions (see below).

We found empirically that a total of 1000 interactions were sufficient to differentiate results under all conditions and to observe convergence between the subjective models and the interaction process (< 5% change in cross entropy).

text.text: Each trial should be understood as an interaction exchange loop starting with the patient expressing their understanding of the situation, thereby modifying the interaction (i.e., observable) process, and to which the clinician responds, thereby modifying the interaction process in turn (see Figure 1 for a flowchart depicting these interactions).

text.text: With each interaction, the patient provides the clinician with information through the selection of an action based on their subjective model, which updates the interaction process influencing subjective observations (e.g., through utterances, "I think 'A' causes my anxiety").

In turn, depending on the conditions, the clinician's reply will lead to a clinical emphasis or deemphasis of certain symptoms-category mappings (e.g.," 'A' generally does/does not cause anxiety"), which also changes the probabilistic structure of the presentation during the interaction (i.e., the interaction process) (see Figure 2).

text.text: Importantly, the symptoms presented by the patient and clinician are biased towards the symptom that they each previously observed (e.g., I was sad/I saw sadness one minute ago, I expect to be/expect to see sadness now) and will shape the observation process accordingly.

As such, the model assumes that symptoms are necessarily linked to an underlying generative process, without committing to the existence of an essentialist diagnostic category underlying their co-occurrence (e.g., depression as a latent entity behind sadness and anxiety) (Kendler et al., 2011).

text.text: Our goal is to explore the effects that looping microdynamics have on the patterns of ascription between the patient and the clinician.

Looping microdynamics may cause the patient and the clinician to reach (or failing to reach) a common ascription of the cause "A" or "B" of the patient's symptom or may cause them to achieve (or fail to achieve) a common ascription of the patient's experienced symptom "sadness" or "anxiety".
We further explore the contribution of looping microdynamics to epistemic injustices.
A "disagreement" over the ascription of categories poses a risk of testimonial injustice (e.g., "I think I have A", "No, you have B", "Yet I really think there is something like A going on").

In turn, a "mismatch" between the patient's reported experience and the clinician's symptom ascription poses a risk of hermeneutical injustice (e.g., "I am feeling sad", "No, this is anxiety", "Ah, OK, but then I'm not sure of what I feel anymore").
We simulate how these risks may be exacerbated in situations of credibility (and intelligibility) deficit on the part of the patient.

In summary, we present a minimal set up to model dyadic exchanges in a patient-clinician context in which the (objective) probability of the patient presenting with a particular symptom or sign, given their clinical diagnosis, depends upon the exchange between the patient and clinician, under their (subjective) generative models.

This setup induces a circular causality characteristic of looping microdynamics which allows the patient-clinician dyad to co-construct an ontology -e.g., through the tendencies of diagnostic categories to elicit certain symptoms and signs (Kotov et al., 2017).

text.text: A POMDP is a mathematical model used to describe decision-making scenarios where the agent has incomplete information about hidden or latent states generating observations.

Unlike a standard MDP model (i.e., a model where the agent has full knowledge of the current state), a POMDP includes observations that provide partial insights into the state, requiring the agent to maintain a belief distribution over possible states.
This model is useful for simulating real-world clinical situations where uncertainty and partial knowledge play a role in decision-making.
The full parametrization of our POMDPs can be found in the code in the appendix.

We implemented 9 conditions -including a baseline -to manipulate the way the patient, and clinician can influence the interaction process directly, and thereby influence each other's subjective model indirectly.
Manipulations under each condition are meant to test the influence of the microdynamics of looping effects on symptom attribution and diagnostic alignment between patients and clinicians.
Conditions 2-5 are "looping" conditions as they involve influences of both the patient and the clinician on the interaction process.

Microdynamic looping effects are driven by patterns of emphasizing and de-emphasizing symptom-category mappings in the interaction process, where deemphasizing means acting -either through behavioral manifestation or speechso as to decrease the probability of a particular symptom in the interaction process (i.e., decreasing the Dirichlet counts in the likelihood mappings in Box 1 by multiplying by .25), and where emphasizing means increasing the Dirichlet counts (i.e., by 2.5).
Conditions 6-9 are "credibility deficit" conditions wherein the patient's ability to modify the interaction process is attenuated (from 2.5 to 1).
The baseline (C1) involves no influence from either side.
In C3 the patient de-emphasizes the likelihood of the interaction process matching his inferred state and observation (e.g., "Dr., I don't think A caused my anxiety").
In response, the clinician emphasizes the likelihood mapping of the interaction process matching her inferred state and observation (e.g., "Well, A usually causes anxiety").
In C4, both the patient and the clinician emphasize the interaction process (e.g., "Dr., I think A caused my anxiety"; "Yes, A usually causes anxiety").
In C5 both the patient and the clinician de-emphasize the interaction process (e.g., "Dr., I don't think A caused my anxiety", "Yes, A rarely causes anxiety").
C6 to C9 are the same as C2 to C5, except that the patient is subject to the credibility deficit described above.

To capture the effect of looping microdynamics on patient-clinician ascription, we measured the number of times the patient and the clinician agreed to elect A or B as the cause of one of the two possible symptoms (i.e., sad or anxious), and the extent to which the patient and the clinician matched in their experience and assessment of the symptoms.

Thus, we operationalized the concept of patient-clinician ascription as patterns of agreements and disagreements over the causes (diagnostic categories A or B) and matches and mismatches over the experience and perception of symptoms (sad or anxious).

Testimonial injustices primarily arise from persistent disagreements over causal attributions, whereas hermeneutical injustices are more likely to emerge from sustained mismatches between patients' lived symptom experience and clinicians' perceptual and interpretative frameworks.
Accordingly, in a situation of credibility deficit, the disconfirmation of the patient's beliefs about the cause of their symptoms can lead to disagreements posing risks of testimonial injustices.
Disconfirmation under credibility deficit can also lead to a mismatch in symptom experience and perception posing additional risks of hermeneutical injustices.
Overall, we assume that epistemic injustice causing harm will tend to happen in disconfirmation conditions.

We thus looked at which of the disconfirmation conditions yielded the most increase (or least decrease) in mismatch, the most increase (or least decrease) in disagreements, and the most increase (or least decrease) in mismatch and disagreements, when compared to baseline.
We also looked at which of the disconfirmation conditions yielded the best results in terms of match agreements.

We found that in the absence of a credibility deficit, negative disconfirmation yielded the least increase in mismatches.
In turn, in the presence of a credibility deficit, positive disconfirmation yielded the most decrease in mismatches.
In the absence of a credibility deficit, both disconfirmation patterns reduced matched and mismatched disagreements to the same degree (1.8% and 1.5% for both C2 and C3).

text.text: Recognizing that failure to reach agreement on the patient's condition may reflect divergent perspectives or the lack of adequate communication between patient and clinician (Heritage & Maynardhttps://paperpile.com/c/1lHXLs/c8BYm 2006) , we presented a model to explore the effect of the microdynamics of looping effects on the alignment of patient-clinician ascription, and their contribution to epistemic injustices using active inference.

text.text: Tracking the way looping microdynamics drives the mutual influence of patients' and clinicians' perspectives is of central importance to identifying successful communication and clinical intervention.
We simulated patient and clinician communicative interaction during interactions under 9 different conditions, including a baseline.
We compared the frequencies of the "patterns of ascription" generated by those microdynamics.

We found that positive confirmation (C8) and positive disconfirmation (C7) under credibility deficit -as well as positive confirmation (C4) in the absence of credibility deficit -yielded the best results with respect to matched agreements.

While disagreements and mismatches are part of ordinary clinical interactions, reaching a common causal attribution may be beneficial in certain contexts, particularly when developing a shared diagnostic formulation or negotiating treatment decisions.
However, such convergence is not necessarily a therapeutic goal in itself.

For instance, in acceptance and commitment therapy (ACT), patients and clinicians may pursue shared therapeutic goals while maintaining different explanations of psychological distress (Hayes et al., 2006).
text.formatted: For instance, in acceptance and commitment therapy (ACT), patients and clinicians may pursue shared therapeutic goals while maintaining different explanations of psychological distress <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Hayes et al., 2006)</ref>.

text.text: Similarly, in the management of medically unexplained symptoms and functional disorders, improving functioning and reducing distress may take precedence over reaching explicit agreement on the underlying causes of symptoms (Kirmayer et al., 2004; Henningsen et al., 2018).
text.formatted: Similarly, in the management of medically unexplained symptoms and functional disorders, improving functioning and reducing distress may take precedence over reaching explicit agreement on the underlying causes of symptoms <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">(Kirmayer et al., 2004;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">Henningsen et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Moreover, consensus itself may sometimes conceal epistemic injustice (e.g., a patient may adopt the clinician's interpretation of their symptoms because of the clinician's perceived authority, even though their own experience remains insufficiently acknowledged).
This is effectively what happens in condition C7, where 99.6% matched agreement is reached due to the fact that the patient's credibility is vitiated.
Thus, matched agreement should be understood as an interactional outcome whose clinical and epistemic value depends on the context.

To examine whether situations in which patients are invalidated in their beliefs and experience may pose enhanced risks of epistemic injustice, we explored how disconfirmation would fare under conditions of credibility deficit.
Interestingly, there was an inverse relationship between negative and positive disconfirmation depending on whether or not a credibility deficit was at play.

The best outcomes in terms of matched agreements, in the absence of credibility deficit, were generated by negative disconfirmation (C2), whereas the best outcomes in matched agreements in the presence of a credibility deficit were produced by positive disconfirmation.

With respect to the risks of testimonial injustice (i.e., risk of category disagreement when invalidating a patient under a credibility deficit), positive disconfirmation was the least risky approach.

With respect to risks of hermeneutical injustices (i.e., risks of symptom perception mismatches when invalidating a patient under a credibility deficit), positive disconfirmation was also the least risky approach.

With respect to combined risks (i.e., risks of symptom perception mismatches and category disagreements when invalidating a patient under a credibility deficit), positive disconfirmation was also the least risky approach.

The main lesson of our study is that in situations of disagreement in which the patient faces a credibility deficit, the clinical approach that minimizes the risks of causing epistemic harm while promoting matched agreement with the patient is that of positive disconfirmation (e.g., "No, it is A that usually causes anxiety") rather than that of negative disconfirmation (e.g., "No, B does not usually cause anxiety").
This interactional effect was revealed by a simple approximate Bayesian update rules in the context of a computer simulation.
Of course, its credibility depends on the adequacy of our model of looping microdynamics and belief formation under active inference.
This work has several technical, conceptual, and clinical limitations.
It relies on a (simplified) active inference architecture with a restricted state-space.
These choices favor transparency and analytical control, to isolate and examine the microdynamics of looping effects without mixing them with higher order sources of variability.
Conceptually, the model presupposes a set of candidate causes (A, B) and treats symptoms (and signs) as observable cues probabilistically related to those causes.
But this does not imply an essentialist view of psychiatric disorders.

Symptoms are understood as any expressed or observed indicators that may support a diagnostic interpretation, which allows the model to remain compatible with non-nosological but pluralistic accounts of psychiatric classification (even though the space of causes is fixed).
Clinically, the model should be understood as a proof of concept rather than a realistic simulation of clinical encounters.

By abstracting away from unexpressed symptoms and individual cognitive biases, we can clarify how looping effects can arise from minimal interactional structures, before reintroducing additional layers of clinical complexity in potential subsequent works.

Additionally, people may hold multiple attributions with different levels of commitment according to past illness experience and symptoms models (Kirmayer, 2026; Kirmayer et al., 1994; Kirmayer & Robbins, 1991).

text.text: It is not clear that our current description of attribution (e.g., P(sad | A) vs.
P(sad | B)) is sufficient to capture such multiple attributions.
Models representing attribution with tensors may be suitable for achieving this (e.g., P(sad | A,B).

6 CONCLUSION As Hacking emphasized, classifications in the human sciences can interact with the people classified, thereby reshaping self-understandings, behaviors, and subsequent classifications through looping effects.
We illustrated how, at the microdynamics level, such looping effects shape clinical interactions.

Our simulations made these looping dynamics explicit by modeling how clinicians' responses, interpretive stances, and diagnostic framings feed back into patients' perceived symptoms, causal attributions, and self-ascription.

Although a computational model could never capture all the complexity of looping dynamics, it can capture some of their foundational principles, allowing us to explore how small, systematic differences in interaction parameters can generate qualitatively different epistemic outcomes over time.
These outcomes can then inform our intuitions about the driving forces of the modelled system.

Indeed, our approach to looping microdynamics supports the intuition that adopting a positive approach -when disconfirming during medical listening -is likely beneficial in clinical exchanges, particularly when patients face credibility deficits.
Listening is central to the relational logic of medical consultation and involves active engagement to elicit symptom and illness narratives (Keller & Carroll, 1994).
text.formatted: Listening is central to the relational logic of medical consultation and involves active engagement to elicit symptom and illness narratives <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">(Keller & Carroll, 1994)</ref>.

text.text: This can be done by restating, paraphrasing and summarizing the patient's discourse (Culley & Bond, 2011).
text.formatted: This can be done by restating, paraphrasing and summarizing the patient's discourse <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Culley & Bond, 2011)</ref>.

text.text: Active listening involves producing cues that indicate when the clinician is paying greater attention to the details of the patient's story (e.g., body language, condition related worries that may be raised, refusal to provide further details, etc.).

Listening to the implicit assumptions of one's own diagnostic line of inquiry while understanding how it may influence the patient's response provides a way to connect with the patient and recognize their concerns.
This points to the larger issue that assessment is not just about diagnosis but establishing an alliance and understanding the patient's predicament.
This can be done by deploying specific patterns of listening, which may result in listening trajectories that depart from the expected consultation trajectory (Cocksedge & May, 2005).
text.formatted: This can be done by deploying specific patterns of listening, which may result in listening trajectories that depart from the expected consultation trajectory <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Cocksedge & May, 2005)</ref>.

text.text: Narrative approaches in clinical care emphasize listening to the broader context of patients' experience in terms of their autobiography, lifeworld, and current concerns (Clark & Mishler, 1992; Kirmayer et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Narrative approaches in clinical care emphasize listening to the broader context of patients' experience in terms of their autobiography, lifeworld, and current concerns <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Clark & Mishler, 1992;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">Kirmayer et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: This may provide rich resources for reframing illness explanations in ways that are epistemically compelling and resonant for patients.
Active listening in clinical interaction must also lead to finding a diagnosis that is consistent with clinical knowledge and that reflects the patient's experience.

This involves confirming and disconfirming aspects of patients' interpretation of events, synthesizing information by linking symptoms to diagnostic categories, discussing the diagnosis transparently, in a collaborative process in which the clinician is flexible and able to re-evaluate and adjust the formulation based on new information.
This interaction can ensure that the diagnosis reflects both clinical observations and the patient's lived experience.

In situations of credibility deficit, additional attention should be paid to the patterns of listening and responding being deployed, as some strategies may pose enhanced risks of epistemic harm, and may lead to a failure to remain responsive to the patient's experience.

Mismatched disagreement: Patient and clinician select different causes and observe different symptoms (e.g., I see anxiety caused by A, you see sadness caused by B): a patient describes anxiety about social interactions as the main reason for avoiding work, attributing their difficulties to social anxiety.
The clinician instead identifies loss of interest and depressive symptoms as the predominant manifestations, favoring an interpretation in terms of depression.
Patient and clinician thus differ both in symptom identification and causal attribution.
